Chapter 10. The Reproduction of Capitalism and the Possibility of Change.
So, let’s take a step back and ask—how does capitalism keep itself going, year after year? And, maybe even more importantly, could it ever really change?
Capitalism isn’t just a system that sits still. It’s constantly being rebuilt—almost like a house that’s never quite finished, with people always hammering away at the structure. This ongoing reproduction happens in a few different, but deeply connected ways.
First, there’s economic reproduction. Every time goods are made and sold, profits aren’t just pocketed and forgotten. They’re reinvested, helping to kickstart the whole process again. Workers come back, ready to sell their labor, and the cycle repeats.
Then, there’s what we call social reproduction. Families, schools, entire communities—they’re all shaping the next wave of workers. They pass on the skills, the habits, and the values that people need to fit into the system.
And let’s not forget ideological reproduction. This is the role of the media, education, and culture. They do more than just inform or entertain us—they subtly teach us that capitalism is normal, even natural. They shape how we see ourselves, and what we think is possible.
But here’s something to pay attention to: none of this happens by magic. Capitalism’s survival isn’t guaranteed. It takes constant work and adjustment. There are always cracks in the system—crises, conflicts, and resistance that threaten to shake things up.
And actually, it’s those very cracks that create opportunities for change. Think about it. When wealth and power become too concentrated, or when work feels meaningless, people start to question things. Recurring crises stir up frustration and inspire folks to imagine alternatives.
Social movements, political action, even small everyday acts of resistance—they all hint at something else being possible.
Let’s look at a hopeful example. Imagine a group of workers in a factory. Instead of just going along with business as usual, they band together, form a cooperative, and take control of production. Now, they’re sharing the rewards of their labor, rather than just clocking in and out. Or picture a neighborhood pushing back against privatization—maybe they reclaim land to use collectively.
Sure, these experiments might be small or face big obstacles, but they show us that other ways of living and working together can exist.
So, what does the future hold for capitalism? That’s not set in stone. This whole system is shaped by what we do—by our choices, our struggles, and our hopes.
If we really understand how capitalism works, we can start to imagine—and maybe even build—something new.
